questions.stem: The nurse is caring for M.L., a 30-year-old client with asthma and right lower lobe pneumonia who was transferred from the ICU yesterday. Refer to the History & Physical, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Click to highlight the findings in the 0300 nurses' note that require immediate follow-up.
questions.passage: Client awake and {{restless, repeatedly pulling at the nasal cannula}}. States, 'I can't catch my breath.' {{Speaking 3–4 words at a time}}. {{Sternocleidomastoid muscles contracting with each breath}}. {{SpO₂ 88% on 2 L/min}}. {{Alert and oriented ×4}}. {{Trachea midline}} with {{symmetric chest expansion}}. {{Coughing thick yellow sputum}}. Reports {{right-sided chest soreness with coughing, 2/10}}. {{Voided 300 mL of clear yellow urine}}.
optionRationales: Requires follow-up — new restlessness and pulling at the oxygen device are early signs of hypoxia, not simple anxiety.
Requires follow-up — speaking only a few words at a time indicates severe dyspnea and high work of breathing.
Requires follow-up — accessory (sternocleidomastoid) muscle use shows the client is struggling to move air; it precedes fatigue.
Requires follow-up — SpO₂ 88% is below the prescribed goal of ≥ 92% and down from 95% five hours ago.
Does not require immediate follow-up — orientation is intact; this is reassuring (though it must be trended).
Does not require immediate follow-up — a midline trachea makes tension pneumothorax (a risk after mechanical ventilation) unlikely.
Does not require immediate follow-up — symmetric expansion argues against pneumothorax or major lobar collapse.
Does not require immediate follow-up — purulent sputum is expected with known bacterial pneumonia already being treated.
Does not require immediate follow-up — mild chest-wall soreness from repeated coughing is expected and rated low.
Does not require immediate follow-up — adequate urine output indicates acceptable perfusion.
questions.rationale: The nurse must separate cues of acute deterioration from findings expected with a known diagnosis. Restlessness, speaking in 3–4 word phrases, accessory muscle use, and a falling SpO₂ below the prescribed target are cues of worsening gas exchange and increasing work of breathing. Purulent sputum and mild cough-related soreness are expected with treated pneumonia, and the midline trachea, symmetric expansion, orientation, and urine output are reassuring.
questions.takeaway: Restlessness + few-word speech + accessory muscles + falling SpO₂ = a client whose breathing is failing.
questions.hintContent: Recall the early signs of hypoxia and the physical signs of increased work of breathing listed in Module 15 (restlessness, speech, posture, muscle use).
questions.hintStrategy: Ask of each phrase: is this NEW or WORSE than expected for a client already known to have pneumonia? Expected findings of a known diagnosis rarely need immediate follow-up.

questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing M.L.'s 0300 assessment. Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. For each finding, indicate whether it is most consistent with the asthma exacerbation, the pneumonia, or both conditions.
rows: Expiratory wheezes in all lung fields
Crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the right lower lobe
PaO₂ 58 mm Hg with SpO₂ 88% on 2 L/min
optionRationales: Asthma — diffuse expiratory wheezing reflects widespread bronchospasm and airway narrowing, not a localized lobar process.
Pneumonia — localized crackles and bronchial breath sounds over one lobe indicate consolidation (alveoli filled with exudate).
Pneumonia — fever reflects the infectious process; an uncomplicated asthma exacerbation does not cause fever.
Asthma — air trapping from narrowed bronchioles lengthens exhalation.
Both — bronchospasm and mucus plugging cause V/Q mismatch, and consolidated alveoli cannot exchange gas; both conditions lower PaO₂.
questions.rationale: M.L. has two interacting problems. Diffuse wheezes and a prolonged expiratory phase are airway (bronchospasm) findings of asthma. Fever and localized crackles with bronchial breath sounds over the RLL are signs of consolidation from pneumonia. Hypoxemia results from both: narrowed airways and consolidated alveoli each create ventilation–perfusion mismatch. Note that the rising WBC is harder to attribute because corticosteroids can also elevate WBC.
questions.takeaway: Diffuse findings point to the airways (asthma); localized findings point to the lobe (pneumonia).
questions.hintContent: Asthma is a diffuse airway disease (bronchospasm, air trapping); pneumonia is an alveolar process that is often localized to a lobe.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort each finding by 'where' and 'why': is it generalized airway narrowing, localized consolidation/infection, or a gas-exchange result both could produce?

questions.stem: The nurse compares M.L.'s 0315 arterial blood gas with the previous results. Refer to the Laboratory Results and Vital Signs. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The client is at highest risk for developing {0} as evidenced by {1}.

options: tension pneumothorax
acute respiratory failure
pulmonary embolism
sepsis-induced hypovolemia
a heart rate of 124/min with a fever
a PaCO₂ that rose from 32 to 47 mm Hg while RR increased
a WBC that rose to 15,800/mm³
right-sided chest soreness with coughing

questions.rationale: Early in an asthma attack, the client hyperventilates and PaCO₂ is low (7.46/32). A 'normal' or rising PaCO₂ in a client who is still breathing 32 times a minute means the respiratory muscles are tiring and ventilation is no longer adequate — a warning sign of impending respiratory failure. Tension pneumothorax is unlikely with a midline trachea and symmetric expansion; tachycardia, fever, WBC, and chest soreness fit the known pneumonia but do not signal the most immediate threat.
questions.takeaway: In acute asthma, a PaCO₂ that climbs back to 'normal' or higher is ominous — the client is tiring.
questions.hintContent: Recall what PaCO₂ is expected to do early in an asthma attack when the client is breathing rapidly, and what it means when PaCO₂ rises despite a high respiratory rate.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the condition first (the most immediate life threat by ABCs), then pick the ONE piece of evidence that best proves that specific condition rather than a finding that fits several problems.

questions.stem: The nurse is planning care for M.L. at 0305. Refer to the Orders and Nurses' Notes. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care at this time? Select all that apply.
options: Administer the PRN albuterol nebulizer treatment
Increase the oxygen flow rate to reach the prescribed SpO₂ goal
Raise the head of the bed to high-Fowler's position
Administer lorazepam 0.5 mg IV for restlessness
Notify the provider of the assessment and ABG findings using SBAR
Hold the methylprednisolone dose because the client is febrile
Place the client flat to decrease oxygen consumption
optionRationales: Correct — a short-acting beta₂-agonist is the first-line reliever for acute bronchospasm; the PRN order covers this.
Correct — the order allows titration to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92%; the current 88% is below goal.
Correct — upright positioning lowers the diaphragm and improves lung expansion.
Incorrect — her restlessness is a sign of hypoxia; a benzodiazepine can depress the respiratory drive of a tiring client.
Correct — worsening hypoxemia and a rising PaCO₂ must be communicated promptly with a clear SBAR report.
Incorrect — systemic corticosteroids are essential to reduce airway inflammation; fever from treated pneumonia is not a reason to hold them without an order.
Incorrect — lying flat pushes abdominal contents against the diaphragm and worsens dyspnea.
questions.rationale: The plan targets bronchospasm (SABA), hypoxemia (titrate oxygen, upright position), and escalation (SBAR to the provider). Sedating a hypoxic, tiring client and holding anti-inflammatory therapy are unsafe, and supine positioning worsens ventilation.
questions.takeaway: For a tiring asthmatic: bronchodilate, oxygenate, sit up, and escalate — never sedate.
questions.hintContent: Review which orders treat bronchospasm, which treat hypoxemia, and which drugs depress respiratory drive.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option on its own: does it improve airway, breathing, or oxygenation right now, or could it harm a client whose ventilation is already failing?

tabs.html:
0300: Restless, speaking 3–4 words at a time, accessory muscle use, diffuse expiratory wheezes, RLL crackles. SpO₂ 88% on 2 L/min.

0310: Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized given. Oxygen increased to 4 L/min. Head of bed raised to high-Fowler's. Provider notified.

0340: Client now drowsy and closes eyes during questioning; arouses to voice. Breath sounds markedly diminished bilaterally with only faint wheezing. Shallow respirations. Skin diaphoretic; lips dusky.

tabs.title: Orders
tabs.html:
• Oxygen by nasal cannula; titrate to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92%
  • Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized every 4 hours and every 1 hour PRN wheezing/dyspnea
  • Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized every 6 hours
  • Methylprednisolone 40 mg IV every 12 hours
  • Ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 hours; azithromycin 500 mg IV every 24 hours
  • Lorazepam 0.5 mg IV every 6 hours PRN anxiety
  • ABG PRN respiratory distress; notify provider for SpO₂ < 90%

questions.stem: The nurse reassesses M.L. at 0340. Refer to the updated Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Allow the client to rest because the slower respirations and quieter wheezing show the nebulizer was effective
Obtain a repeat arterial blood gas and wait for the results before calling for assistance
Activate the rapid response team and stay with the client
Administer the next dose of methylprednisolone early to reduce airway inflammation
optionRationales: Incorrect — a 'quiet chest' with diminished breath sounds, drowsiness, and falling RR signals exhaustion and minimal airflow, not improvement.
Incorrect — delaying help to obtain data wastes time; the clinical picture already indicates respiratory failure.
Correct — drowsiness, shallow RR of 14, diminished breath sounds, and SpO₂ 84% on 6 L/min indicate impending respiratory arrest; the client needs immediate advanced airway support.
Incorrect — corticosteroids take hours to work, and giving a dose early requires an order; they will not reverse imminent arrest.
questions.rationale: A decreasing respiratory rate with decreased wheezing and falling level of consciousness in a client with severe asthma is a sign of respiratory muscle fatigue and CO₂ narcosis, not improvement. The priority is to summon the rapid response team (and prepare to assist ventilation with a bag-valve mask) while remaining with the client. Waiting for an ABG or giving slow-acting drugs delays life-saving care.
questions.takeaway: A 'silent chest' in asthma is an emergency — call for help, don't celebrate.
questions.hintContent: Recall why wheezing may fade and respiratory rate may fall as a severe asthma attack WORSENS.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare the 0340 data with 0300. The word 'first' plus a declining level of consciousness means choose the action that brings the most help the fastest.

tabs.title: Progress Note
tabs.html: Hospital day 9, 0900: M.L. was transferred to the ICU on day 3, reintubated for 48 hours, and returned to the medical unit on day 6. Sputum culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae sensitive to ceftriaxone. Methylprednisolone changed to prednisone 40 mg PO daily.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Day 9, 0800: Awake, alert, speaking in full sentences. Ambulated 150 ft in the hallway on room air. Used albuterol MDI once in the past 24 hours. Faint expiratory wheezes on forced exhalation only. Breath sounds absent at the right base with dullness to percussion; client reports new right-sided chest pain on deep inspiration, 5/10.

questions.stem: M.L. is now on hospital day 9. Refer to the Progress Note, Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. For each finding, indicate whether it shows that treatment has been effective or ineffective (requires follow-up).
rows: Speaking in full sentences and ambulating 150 ft on room air
Peak expiratory flow 84% of personal best
Absent breath sounds and dullness to percussion at the right base
optionRationales: Effective — full sentences and activity tolerance on room air show improved ventilation and gas exchange.
Effective — resolution of fever and leukocytosis indicates the antibiotic is controlling the infection.
Effective — ≥ 80% of personal best is the green zone of an asthma action plan.
Ineffective — absent breath sounds with dullness at the base suggest a pleural effusion or empyema complicating pneumonia and must be reported.
Ineffective — new pleuritic pain accompanying basal dullness supports a pleural complication and requires follow-up.
questions.rationale: Most outcome criteria are met: improved speech and activity, afebrile with normal WBC, and PEF in the green zone. However, new dullness and absent breath sounds at the right base with pleuritic pain are not expected in resolving pneumonia; they suggest a parapneumonic effusion or empyema and need provider notification and likely imaging.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate every finding against the goal — one new abnormal finding can hide among many improving ones.
questions.hintContent: Recall the expected outcome criteria for asthma (PEF zones, speech, activity) and pneumonia (temperature, WBC, breath sounds), and what dullness to percussion indicates.
questions.hintStrategy: Judge each row independently against the goal of treatment; don't let the overall improving trend make you mark a NEW abnormal finding as effective.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
1410: 34-year-old client admitted 6 hours ago after a motor vehicle crash with right rib fractures (ribs 5–7) and a right pneumothorax. Right chest tube to –20 cm H₂O dry suction placed in the ED. Returned from CT scan at 1400; transport staff placed a clamp on the chest tube 'for safety' during transfer.

1425: Client reports sudden, severe shortness of breath and says 'something is wrong.' Anxious and diaphoretic. Trachea deviated to the left. Absent breath sounds on the right. Neck veins distended. No tidaling or bubbling in the water seal chamber.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes and Vital Signs. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

options: Cardiac tamponade
Pulmonary embolism
Tension pneumothorax
Massive hemothorax
Remove the clamp from the chest tube
Milk and strip the chest tube toward the drainage unit
Raise the drainage unit to the level of the bed for easier observation
Call the rapid response team and prepare for emergency decompression
Place the client in Trendelenburg position to raise the blood pressure
Tracheal position and right-sided breath sounds
Serum amylase level
Blood pressure and heart rate
Hourly urine specific gravity
Capillary blood glucose

condition: Incorrect — tamponade causes JVD and hypotension but not tracheal deviation or absent unilateral breath sounds.
Incorrect — PE causes sudden dyspnea and tachycardia but breath sounds are usually present and the trachea is midline.
Correct — a clamped chest tube traps air in the pleural space; tracheal deviation away from the affected side, absent breath sounds, JVD, and hypotension are classic tension pneumothorax.
Incorrect — massive hemothorax causes absent breath sounds and shock, but neck veins are typically flat from blood loss, and the scenario cause is a clamped tube.
actions: Correct — the clamp is the cause; removing it restores the path for trapped air to escape.
Incorrect — stripping creates dangerous negative pressure and does not address the clamp; it is not routinely recommended.
Incorrect — the drainage unit must stay below chest level to prevent backflow into the pleural space.
Correct — hemodynamic compromise needs immediate provider response; needle decompression or a new tube may be needed if unclamping does not relieve it.
Incorrect — head-down positioning worsens dyspnea; the client should be upright if BP allows.
parameters: Correct — return of the trachea to midline and return of breath sounds show the pleural air has been evacuated.
Incorrect — amylase is unrelated to the pleural space.
Correct — rising BP and falling HR show venous return and cardiac output are recovering.
Incorrect — urine specific gravity is not a direct indicator of this emergency's resolution.
Incorrect — glucose is not affected by the pneumothorax.

questions.rationale: Clamping a chest tube that is draining air from a pneumothorax allows air to accumulate under pressure, collapsing the lung and shifting the mediastinum. This compresses the heart and great vessels, reducing venous return (JVD, hypotension). The nurse removes the clamp immediately and summons emergency help; progress is shown by midline trachea, returning breath sounds, and improving hemodynamics.
questions.takeaway: Never clamp a chest tube for transport — a clamped tube can turn a pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax.
questions.hintContent: Recall what happens when air continues to leak into the pleural space but has no exit, and which way the mediastinum shifts.
questions.hintStrategy: Start in the middle: link the most specific cues (tracheal shift, JVD, absent breath sounds, a clamp) to one condition. Then pick actions that treat THAT cause and parameters that directly reflect its resolution.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html: Emergency department, 1120: 74-year-old client with severe COPD (home O₂ 2 L/min) brought in by family for 3 days of increased dyspnea and cough with thick green sputum. Family reports the client 'has been sleepier than usual today.' Client is drowsy but arouses to voice, sitting in tripod position, pursed-lip breathing, using accessory muscles. Diffuse expiratory wheezes with diminished bases. Arrived on home O₂ at 2 L/min by nasal cannula.

questions.stem: Refer to the Nurses' Notes, Vital Signs, and Laboratory Results. Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take to address that condition, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.

options: Metabolic alkalosis from diuretic therapy
COPD exacerbation with acute hypercapnic respiratory failure
Acute pulmonary edema from left-sided heart failure
Spontaneous pneumothorax
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min to raise SpO₂ to 100%
Administer PRN morphine to relieve air hunger
Titrate oxygen to a target SpO₂ of 88%–92%
Prepare the client for noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation (BiPAP)
Encourage the client to lie supine to rest the respiratory muscles
Level of consciousness
Serum sodium
Daily weight
Repeat ABG pH and PaCO₂
Peak expiratory flow rate

condition: Incorrect — the pH is acidotic, not alkalotic; the elevated HCO₃⁻ is chronic renal compensation.
Correct — increased dyspnea, purulent sputum, drowsiness, and pH 7.28 with PaCO₂ 72 and a compensatory HCO₃⁻ indicate acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis during a COPD exacerbation.
Incorrect — pulmonary edema would present with crackles and frothy sputum rather than green sputum and wheezes.
Incorrect — pneumothorax causes unilateral absent breath sounds and sudden pleuritic pain, not diffuse wheezes.
actions: Incorrect — high-concentration oxygen in a CO₂ retainer worsens hypercapnia (V/Q changes, Haldane effect) and may deepen somnolence; oxygen should be increased only enough to reach the target.
Incorrect — opioids depress respiratory drive in a client already retaining CO₂.
Correct — the evidence-based SpO₂ target for COPD exacerbation is 88%–92%, using controlled oxygen.
Correct — NIV is recommended for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH ≤ 7.35, PaCO₂ > 45) and reduces the need for intubation.
Incorrect — supine positioning impairs diaphragmatic movement; COPD clients breathe best upright or leaning forward.
parameters: Correct — improving alertness shows falling CO₂ levels; worsening drowsiness signals failure of NIV.
Incorrect — sodium does not reflect ventilation.
Incorrect — weight trends fluid status, not acute CO₂ retention.
Correct — a rising pH and falling PaCO₂ on repeat ABG are the objective measures of improved ventilation.
Incorrect — PEF is effort dependent and not reliable in a drowsy client with an exacerbation; it is primarily an asthma self-monitoring tool.

questions.rationale: The client has a COPD exacerbation (increased dyspnea, sputum volume and purulence) with acute-on-chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, with hypoxemia below the COPD target. Care focuses on controlled oxygen (SpO₂ 88%–92%) and noninvasive ventilation, with bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics as prescribed. Level of consciousness and serial ABGs show whether ventilation is improving.
questions.takeaway: COPD + drowsy + high PaCO₂: target SpO₂ 88%–92% and think BiPAP.
questions.hintContent: Recall the GOLD oxygen target for COPD exacerbations and the ABG pattern of acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis (low pH, high PaCO₂, elevated HCO₃⁻).
questions.hintStrategy: Interpret the ABG first to name the condition. Then eliminate any action that would further suppress ventilation or raise CO₂, and choose parameters that directly measure ventilation.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 67-year-old client on postoperative day 2 after an open colon resection. Refer to the Vital Signs and Medication Administration Record. Click to highlight the findings in the nurse's assessment that indicate ineffective airway clearance.
questions.passage: Client is {{resting in a semi-reclined position with the head of bed at 15°}}. States, 'It hurts too much to cough, so I just clear my throat.' {{Incentive spirometer volume 500 mL; preoperative goal 1,500 mL}}. {{Diminished breath sounds with fine crackles in both bases}} that {{do not clear with coughing}}. {{Abdominal incision edges approximated without drainage}}. {{Bowel sounds hypoactive in all 4 quadrants}}. {{Pedal pulses 2+ bilaterally}}. {{Oral mucosa dry; drank 240 mL since 0000}}. {{Oriented to person, place, and time}}.
optionRationales: Not an airway-clearance cue itself — the low head of bed is a contributing risk factor (poor lung expansion) to correct, but it is a position, not evidence of retained secretions.
Indicates ineffective airway clearance — a volume far below the goal shows shallow breathing and inadequate lung expansion, which allows secretions to pool.
Indicates ineffective airway clearance — diminished bases with crackles on POD 2 suggest atelectasis and retained secretions.
Indicates ineffective airway clearance — crackles that persist after coughing show the cough is not mobilizing secretions.
Not related — a well-approximated incision is an expected finding.
Not related — hypoactive bowel sounds are expected after bowel surgery and reflect GI, not respiratory, function.
Not related — pedal pulses reflect peripheral perfusion.
Indicates ineffective airway clearance — dehydration thickens secretions, making them harder to expectorate.
Not related — orientation is intact; confusion would be a later sign of hypoxia.
questions.rationale: Pain-limited coughing, low incentive spirometer volumes, and bibasilar crackles that do not clear with coughing are the defining cues of ineffective airway clearance and early atelectasis — reinforced by a new low-grade fever, tachypnea, and SpO₂ drop in the exhibit. Poor fluid intake thickens secretions. The nurse should medicate for pain, teach splinted coughing, raise the head of the bed, encourage fluids, and ambulate the client.
questions.takeaway: Postoperative atelectasis: low IS volumes + basal crackles + pain-limited cough + POD 1–2 fever.
questions.hintContent: Recall the defining characteristics of ineffective airway clearance: ineffective cough, adventitious sounds, and factors that thicken or retain secretions.
questions.hintStrategy: Highlight only the findings that are EVIDENCE of retained secretions or inadequate lung expansion — not every abnormal finding and not risk factors that describe positioning or other systems.

questions.passage: Client reports {{smoking since age 16}} and {{two previous quit attempts using nicotine gum}}. Medical history includes {{a seizure after a head injury 4 years ago}} and {{seasonal allergic rhinitis}}. Client states, {{'I usually have 3 or 4 beers every night to help me sleep'}} and plans {{to stop drinking completely when I quit smoking}}. Current medications: {{loratadine 10 mg daily}} and {{phenelzine, started last year for depression}}. Client {{works night shifts as a security guard}}.
optionRationales: Not a contraindication — long smoking history is the reason for treatment.
Not a contraindication — prior NRT use is helpful history for planning combination therapy.
Report — bupropion lowers the seizure threshold; a seizure history is a contraindication.
Not a contraindication — allergic rhinitis does not interact with bupropion.
Monitor — regular alcohol use should be discussed, but the dangerous feature is abrupt discontinuation (next segment).
Report — abrupt discontinuation of heavy alcohol use while starting bupropion greatly increases seizure risk.
Not a contraindication — loratadine has no significant interaction with bupropion.
Report — phenelzine is an MAOI; bupropion is contraindicated within 14 days of an MAOI (risk of hypertensive reaction).
Not a contraindication — shift work affects sleep planning and dosing times but does not prohibit use.
questions.rationale: Bupropion is contraindicated in clients with a seizure disorder, a current or prior eating disorder, use of an MAOI within 14 days, and abrupt discontinuation of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or antiseizure drugs, because each raises the risk of seizures or hypertensive reactions. This client has three such findings and needs a different cessation plan (e.g., varenicline or combination NRT) decided with the provider.
questions.takeaway: Bupropion: screen for seizures, eating disorders, MAOIs, and abrupt alcohol/sedative withdrawal.
questions.hintContent: Recall bupropion's major contraindications — most relate to lowering the seizure threshold, plus one drug-class interaction.
questions.hintStrategy: For each phrase, ask: does this make bupropion UNSAFE for this client? Highlight only true contraindications, not general risk factors or neutral history.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 52-year-old client admitted 12 hours ago with an asthma exacerbation. Refer to the Medication Administration Record and Laboratory Results. Click to highlight the findings in the assessment that require follow-up with the provider.

Reports {{new palpitations; apical pulse irregular with frequent skipped beats}}. {{Leg muscles feel weak and crampy}}. {{Wheezes decreased from yesterday}}. {{Voice slightly hoarse}}. {{Speaking in full sentences}}. {{Fingerstick glucose before lunch 274 mg/dL}}.
optionRationales: Expected — fine tremor is a common beta₂-agonist adverse effect and not dangerous by itself.
Expected — nervousness is a common, self-limiting effect of albuterol.
Expected — mild tachycardia is common with frequent albuterol and during an exacerbation.
Requires follow-up — palpitations with an irregular rhythm in a client with K⁺ 3.0 suggest hypokalemia-related dysrhythmia (albuterol and corticosteroids both lower potassium).
Requires follow-up — muscle weakness and cramps are manifestations of hypokalemia.
Expected — decreasing wheezes indicate improvement.
Expected — mild hoarseness is a local effect of inhaled corticosteroids and of the illness; teach mouth rinsing.
Expected — full sentences indicate improving respiratory status.

Systemic corticosteroids also cause hyperglycemia. Tremor, jitteriness, and mild tachycardia are expected albuterol effects.

questions.hintContent: Recall the electrolyte effect of repeated beta₂-agonist doses and the metabolic effects of systemic corticosteroids.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: An 82-year-old client who had a stroke 2 days ago has a weak cough and a diminished gag reflex. The nurse hears gurgling with each breath and sees secretions pooled in the mouth. SpO₂ is 91% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Offer small sips of water to help the client clear the throat
Suction the mouth and pharynx with a Yankauer (tonsil-tip) catheter
Perform nasotracheal suctioning with a sterile catheter right away
Increase the oxygen to 4 L/min and recheck the SpO₂ in 15 minutes
optionRationales: Incorrect — oral fluids for a client with a diminished gag reflex and pooled secretions greatly increase the risk of aspiration; a swallow screen is required before any oral intake.

Correct — the secretions are visible in the mouth and pharynx, so oropharyngeal suctioning with a rigid Yankauer catheter is the least invasive effective way to clear the airway. Turning the client to the side also helps secretions drain.
Incorrect — nasotracheal suctioning is more invasive and is used for secretions in the trachea that cannot be cleared otherwise; these secretions are in the mouth.
Incorrect — more oxygen does not clear the obstruction, and waiting 15 minutes leaves the client at risk for aspiration.
questions.rationale: Older adults and clients after a stroke have a weaker cough and gag reflex, so secretions pool and are easily aspirated — the module lists frequent suctioning as a treatment for this reason. When secretions are visible in the mouth, the nurse clears the airway with oropharyngeal (Yankauer) suctioning, positions the client side-lying or with the head of the bed elevated, and then reassesses breath sounds and SpO₂. The least invasive method that reaches the secretions is used first.
questions.takeaway: Secretions pooled in the mouth of a client with a weak gag reflex: suction with a Yankauer first, then reassess.
questions.hintContent: Recall why older adults with a decreased gag reflex need frequent suctioning, and how far each type of suction catheter reaches.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify where the secretions are located. The first action should clear them with the least invasive method that reaches that location.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the huff (forced expiratory) cough technique to a client with COPD who has thick secretions and tires easily with regular coughing. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Assist the client to sit upright with feet supported and shoulders relaxed
Have the client take a slow, medium-sized breath through the nose
Instruct the client to hold the breath for 2–3 seconds
Have the client exhale forcefully through an open mouth, saying 'huff'
Repeat 2–3 times, then have the client cough to expel loosened mucus
questions.rationale: Upright posture maximizes diaphragmatic excursion. A medium breath with a brief hold allows air to move behind secretions through collateral ventilation. A forceful open-mouth 'huff' moves mucus toward larger airways without the high pressures that cause airway collapse in COPD, and a final cough clears it.
questions.takeaway: Huff coughing: sit up, medium breath, hold, 'huff' with an open mouth, then cough.
questions.hintContent: Recall why huffing is gentler than a closed-glottis cough for clients with airways that collapse easily.
questions.hintStrategy: Build the sequence logically: position → inhale → hold → exhale technique → finishing step.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 70-year-old client admitted with pneumonia who has thick, tenacious sputum that is difficult to expectorate. The client has no history of heart or kidney failure. Which interventions should the nurse include to promote airway clearance? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage oral fluid intake of 2–3 L/day
Assist the client to ambulate in the hallway three times daily
Administer a cough suppressant every 4 hours around the clock
Provide humidified oxygen as prescribed
Keep the client supine to conserve energy
Offer an antihistamine at bedtime to dry secretions
optionRationales: Correct — adequate hydration thins secretions so they are easier to cough up.
Correct — mobility increases lung expansion and mobilizes secretions.
Incorrect — suppressing a productive cough causes retention of secretions.
Correct — humidification prevents drying of the airway mucosa and thickening of mucus.
Incorrect — immobility and supine positioning promote pooling of secretions and atelectasis.
Incorrect — antihistamines thicken secretions and make them harder to clear.
questions.rationale: Airway clearance improves when secretions are thinned (fluids, humidification) and mobilized (ambulation, position changes, effective coughing). Suppressing a productive cough, drying secretions with antihistamines, and immobility all promote mucus retention.
questions.takeaway: Thin it (fluids, humidity), move it (ambulate, turn), and cough it out — don't suppress it.
questions.hintContent: Think about the two goals of airway-clearance care: make secretions thinner and help move them out of the lungs.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option independently: does it thin or mobilize secretions, or does it thicken or trap them?

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with bronchiectasis is taught to use an oscillating positive expiratory pressure (PEP) device (e.g., a flutter valve) twice daily. Which statement by the client indicates the teaching was effective?
options: 'I will breathe in forcefully through the device, like my incentive spirometer, to open up my lungs.'
'I will use the device only when I feel short of breath, the same way I would use a rescue inhaler.'
'I will lie flat on my back while using it so the vibrations can reach the bottom of my lungs.'
'I'll take a bigger breath, hold it, breathe out steadily through the device, then huff.'
optionRationales: Incorrect — oscillating PEP devices work on exhalation; inhaling through them is incorrect technique.
Incorrect — the device is scheduled airway-clearance therapy, not a reliever for dyspnea.
Incorrect — the client should sit upright; lying flat reduces lung volumes.
Correct — a larger breath with a 2–3 second hold, then active exhalation through the device creates vibrations that loosen mucus, followed by huff coughing to clear it.
questions.rationale: Oscillating PEP devices create back-pressure and vibrations during exhalation that splint airways open and loosen mucus from airway walls. The technique is a larger-than-normal breath, a brief hold, and an active (not maximal) exhalation through the device for a series of breaths, followed by huff coughs.
questions.takeaway: Oscillating PEP works on the exhale — breathe in, hold, blow out through the device, then huff.
questions.hintContent: Recall on which phase of breathing a PEP device generates its therapeutic pressure and vibration.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a teaching-evaluation item looking for the CORRECT statement. Eliminate statements that confuse the device with other respiratory equipment.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: The nurse is positioning several clients to support oxygenation and protect the airway. For each positioning plan, indicate whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Client at 34 weeks' gestation with pneumonia and dyspnea: semi-Fowler's position with a wedge under the right hip
Client with acute pulmonary edema: high-Fowler's position with the legs dependent
Drowsy client with a weak gag reflex who is vomiting: flat supine position
Client receiving continuous tube feedings: head of the bed at 10°
Postoperative client with atelectasis: keep in the same position to limit incisional pain
optionRationales: Indicated — upright positioning eases dyspnea, and a lateral tilt keeps the uterus off the vena cava; the module warns against prolonged supine positioning in pregnancy.
Indicated — sitting upright with the legs down lowers the diaphragm and reduces venous return, which decreases pulmonary congestion.
Not indicated — a client who cannot protect the airway should be turned to the side so vomitus drains from the mouth instead of into the trachea.
Not indicated — the head of the bed should be at least 30° during tube feedings to reduce reflux and aspiration.
Not indicated — immobility worsens atelectasis; the client needs pain control, turning every 2 hours, and early ambulation.
questions.rationale: Positioning is an independent nursing intervention that improves lung expansion and prevents aspiration. Upright positions lower the diaphragm; a lateral tilt protects venous return in late pregnancy; side-lying protects the airway of a client who is vomiting with a weak gag reflex; a head-of-bed elevation of at least 30° reduces aspiration during tube feeding; and frequent position changes prevent atelectasis.
questions.takeaway: Position for the problem: upright for dyspnea, tilt in late pregnancy, side-lying if vomiting, HOB ≥ 30° with tube feeds, and keep postoperative clients moving.
questions.hintContent: Recall how each position affects diaphragm movement, venous return, and the risk of aspirating stomach contents.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row, identify the main risk for that client (poor lung expansion, a compressed vena cava, or aspiration) and ask whether the position reduces it.

questions.stem: The RN is working with a licensed practical nurse (LPN) and an unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) on a respiratory unit. Which tasks are appropriate for the RN to delegate? Select all that apply.
options: UAP: assist a stable client with pneumonia to ambulate in the hallway
LPN: perform tracheostomy suctioning for a stable client with a long-term tracheostomy
UAP: evaluate whether a client's dyspnea improved after a nebulizer treatment
LPN: perform the initial admission assessment of a client with a new pneumothorax
UAP: remind a postoperative client to use the incentive spirometer every hour
LPN: develop the discharge teaching plan for a client newly diagnosed with COPD
optionRationales: Appropriate — ambulating a stable client is within UAP scope.
Appropriate — suctioning a stable client with an established tracheostomy is a routine skill within LPN scope.
Not appropriate — evaluating the response to treatment requires RN assessment.
Not appropriate — initial assessment of a new, potentially unstable client is an RN responsibility.
Appropriate — reminding a client to perform a previously taught activity is within UAP scope; the RN evaluates technique.
Not appropriate — developing a teaching plan requires RN judgment; the LPN may reinforce it.
questions.rationale: The RN retains assessment, evaluation, initial teaching, and care planning. Stable clients with predictable outcomes and routine procedures (ambulation, reminders, established trach suctioning) can be delegated to the appropriately trained team member.
questions.takeaway: Delegate tasks, not judgment: assess, plan, teach, and evaluate stay with the RN.
questions.hintContent: Recall the five rights of delegation and which nursing process steps cannot be delegated.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the verbs — 'evaluate,' 'initial assessment,' and 'develop a plan' signal RN-only work; also weigh whether the client is stable.

questions.stem: The nurse prepares to perform open tracheal suctioning for an adult client with a tracheostomy who has coarse rhonchi over the trachea and an SpO₂ of 90%. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: Before suctioning, the nurse should hyperoxygenate the client with {0}, set the wall suction pressure to {1}, and limit each suction pass to {2}.

options: 100% oxygen for 30–60 seconds
room air for 2 minutes
the current FiO₂ for 5 seconds
a nebulized saline bolus
40–60 mm Hg
no longer than 10–15 seconds
30 seconds
until the client stops coughing
60 seconds

questions.rationale: Hyperoxygenating with 100% oxygen for 30–60 seconds limits suction-induced hypoxemia. Adult suction pressure of about 100–150 mm Hg removes secretions while limiting mucosal trauma and atelectasis. Each pass lasting no more than 10–15 seconds prevents hypoxemia and vagal bradycardia. Routine saline instillation is not recommended.
questions.takeaway: Suction safely: 100% O₂ first, 100–150 mm Hg, ≤ 10–15 seconds per pass.
questions.hintContent: Recall the evidence-based adult suctioning parameters that prevent hypoxemia, mucosal trauma, and atelectasis.
questions.hintStrategy: For each blank, eliminate extremes that would clearly cause harm (too high pressure, too long a pass) or be ineffective.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old client with persistent asthma was started on montelukast 10 mg every evening 3 weeks ago. At a follow-up visit, the parent reports that the adolescent has had nightmares, is newly irritable, and has been withdrawn from friends. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Report the findings to the provider promptly
Instruct the parent to give the dose in the morning instead
Reassure the parent that mood changes are normal during adolescence
Explain that these effects resolve after the first month of therapy
optionRationales: Correct — montelukast carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events (nightmares, agitation, depression, suicidal thinking); the provider must evaluate and likely discontinue it.
Incorrect — changing dose timing does not address neuropsychiatric effects and is outside nursing scope without an order.
Incorrect — attributing new symptoms to adolescence ignores a known serious adverse effect.
Incorrect — these effects do not reliably resolve and may progress to suicidal ideation.
questions.rationale: Leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast can cause serious neuropsychiatric effects, including sleep disturbances, agitation, depression, and suicidal thoughts, which led to an FDA boxed warning. New behavior changes after starting the drug must be reported promptly, and families should be taught to watch for them from the start of therapy.
questions.takeaway: Montelukast: teach families to report nightmares, mood changes, or suicidal thoughts.
questions.hintContent: Recall the boxed warning associated with leukotriene receptor antagonists.
questions.hintStrategy: When new symptoms follow a new medication, consider an adverse drug effect before attributing them to age or normal development.

Albuterol
Budesonide
Sertraline
optionRationales: Correct — propranolol is a nonselective beta blocker; blocking beta₂ receptors in the bronchioles can cause bronchospasm and blunt the effect of albuterol.
Incorrect — a SABA reliever is appropriate for asthma.
Incorrect — an inhaled corticosteroid is the foundation of asthma control therapy.
Incorrect — sertraline has no significant bronchoconstrictive effect.

questions.hintContent: Recall which receptor causes bronchodilation and which drugs block it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with type 2 diabetes is admitted with an asthma exacerbation and is prescribed methylprednisolone 60 mg IV every 6 hours. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Monitor capillary blood glucose before meals and at bedtime
Monitor serum potassium levels
Expect the medication to relieve wheezing within 5 minutes
Assess for signs of infection, recognizing fever may be blunted
Stop the medication abruptly once wheezing resolves
Monitor for mood changes and insomnia
optionRationales: Correct — corticosteroids raise blood glucose, especially in clients with diabetes.
Correct — corticosteroids promote potassium loss; hypokalemia is compounded by frequent beta₂-agonists.
Incorrect — systemic corticosteroids reduce inflammation over hours; they are not rapid bronchodilators.
Correct — immunosuppression increases infection risk and can mask fever and inflammation.
Incorrect — the provider tapers or converts to oral therapy; clients should not abruptly stop corticosteroids without a prescriber's plan.
Correct — steroid-induced psychiatric effects include insomnia, euphoria, agitation, and mood swings.
questions.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are essential in moderate-to-severe exacerbations but cause hyperglycemia, hypokalemia, immunosuppression with masked infection, and neuropsychiatric effects. Their anti-inflammatory benefit begins over several hours, so SABAs provide the rapid relief. Discontinuation follows a prescribed plan.
questions.takeaway: Systemic steroids: watch glucose, potassium, infection, and mood — and don't expect instant relief.
questions.hintContent: Recall the metabolic, immune, and CNS effects of systemic glucocorticoids and how fast they work.
questions.hintStrategy: Consider each option alone: does it monitor for a real adverse effect, or does it reflect a misconception about onset or discontinuation?

questions.stem: The nurse observes a client with COPD demonstrating the use of a new fluticasone/salmeterol dry powder inhaler (disk device). Which action by the client requires the nurse to intervene?
options: Holds the device level after sliding the lever to load the dose
Exhales fully into the mouthpiece before inhaling the dose
Inhales quickly and deeply through the mouthpiece
Rinses the mouth with water and spits after the dose
optionRationales: Incorrect — keeping the device level after loading prevents loss of the powder; this is correct technique.
Correct — exhaling into a dry powder inhaler blows moisture into it and can disperse the powder, so the client receives an incomplete dose; exhale away from the device.
Incorrect — DPIs require a quick, forceful, deep inhalation to draw the powder into the lungs.
Incorrect — rinsing and spitting after an inhaled corticosteroid reduces the risk of oral candidiasis and hoarseness.
questions.rationale: Dry powder inhalers are breath-activated and require a rapid, deep inhalation. They are not shaken and are not used with a spacer. The client should exhale away from the mouthpiece, because moisture from breath clumps the powder and blows the dose out. After an ICS-containing inhaler, the client rinses and spits.
questions.takeaway: DPI: exhale away, seal lips, breathe in fast and deep, rinse and spit.
questions.hintContent: Recall how a dry powder inhaler delivers medication differently from a pressurized MDI.
questions.hintStrategy: The item asks which action needs INTERVENTION — look for the one incorrect step among correct steps.

questions.stem: The nurse is administering albuterol 2.5 mg by small-volume nebulizer to a client with wheezing. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Verify the prescription and identify the client using two identifiers
Assess baseline heart rate, breath sounds, and SpO₂
Add the medication to the nebulizer cup and connect it to the gas source at 6–8 L/min
Instruct the client to sit upright and breathe slowly and deeply through the mouthpiece until the mist stops
Reassess heart rate, breath sounds, and SpO₂ after the treatment
questions.rationale: Safe administration starts with verifying the order and client identity, then obtaining baseline data for later comparison. The nebulizer is prepared with an adequate flow to generate mist, and upright slow deep breathing maximizes deposition in the lower airways. Reassessment evaluates effectiveness (breath sounds, SpO₂) and adverse effects (tachycardia).
questions.takeaway: Baseline → treat → reassess: you can't evaluate a bronchodilator without a before-and-after.
questions.hintContent: Recall the nursing process as applied to medication administration: safety checks, baseline assessment, administration, evaluation.
questions.hintStrategy: Anchor the first and last steps first (safety check and evaluation), then order the middle steps logically.

questions.stem: A client with allergic asthma receives a scheduled allergen immunotherapy (allergy shot) injection in the clinic. Ten minutes later, the client reports throat tightness and itching. The nurse notes hives on the chest, audible wheezing, HR 118/min, and BP 86/50 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer an oral antihistamine and observe for 30 minutes
Administer the client's albuterol inhaler 2 puffs
Apply ice to the injection site to slow absorption
Administer epinephrine intramuscularly per protocol
optionRationales: Incorrect — antihistamines relieve hives but do not reverse airway edema or hypotension; they are adjuncts only.
Incorrect — albuterol may help wheezing but does not treat the systemic reaction or hypotension.
Incorrect — local measures do not treat systemic anaphylaxis.
Correct — hives with airway symptoms and hypotension after allergen exposure is anaphylaxis; IM epinephrine is the first-line, life-saving treatment.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis is a known risk of allergen immunotherapy, which is why clients are observed for at least 30 minutes after each injection in a setting with emergency equipment. Multisystem signs (skin, airway, hypotension) require immediate IM epinephrine, which reverses bronchoconstriction, laryngeal edema, and vasodilation. Antihistamines, bronchodilators, oxygen, and fluids are adjuncts.
questions.takeaway: Anaphylaxis = epinephrine IM first; everything else is second.
questions.hintContent: Recall the first-line drug for anaphylaxis and why adjunct drugs are not enough.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the condition from the cluster of cues, then select the single action that reverses the most life-threatening problems at once.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the home medications of a 25-year-old client with asthma who says, 'I get confused about which inhaler to use when I'm wheezing.' For each medication, indicate whether it is a quick-relief (rescue) medication or a long-term control medication for this client.
optionRationales: Quick-relief — a short-acting beta₂-agonist works within minutes to relieve bronchospasm.
Long-term control — inhaled corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation over days to weeks.
Long-term control — a leukotriene modifier is taken daily for prevention and does not relieve an acute attack.

Long-term control — salmeterol is a long-acting beta₂-agonist with a slow onset, so salmeterol/fluticasone must never be used for rescue. (Under GINA, only an ICS–formoterol combination may also serve as a reliever.)
Quick-relief — levalbuterol is a short-acting beta₂-agonist (the R-isomer of albuterol).
questions.rationale: This item uses the textbook's (NAEPP-based) classification: short-acting beta₂-agonists (albuterol, levalbuterol) are quick-relief drugs, while inhaled corticosteroids, ICS/salmeterol combinations, and leukotriene modifiers are long-term controllers taken daily regardless of symptoms. Current GINA guidance differs in one important way: it no longer recommends SABA-only treatment for adolescents and adults, and its preferred reliever is as-needed low-dose ICS–formoterol, often used as both maintenance and reliever therapy (MART). Formoterol has a rapid onset, so that combination can act as a reliever; salmeterol does not, so salmeterol/fluticasone remains a controller only. Among this client's inhalers, albuterol and levalbuterol are the relievers.
questions.takeaway: Rescue = SABA (or, per GINA, ICS–formoterol); controllers such as ICS and ICS/salmeterol are taken every day, even when well.
questions.hintContent: Recall the onset of action of short-acting versus long-acting beta₂-agonists, corticosteroids, and leukotriene modifiers.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify each drug by drug class first, then by how fast it works.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing the Clinic Note for a client with asthma. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The client's findings indicate {0} asthma. The nurse should anticipate that the provider will {1}.

options: well-controlled
not well-controlled
exercise-induced only
resolving
add daily inhaled corticosteroid–containing controller therapy
add a long-acting beta₂-agonist as the only new medication
increase the albuterol to every 2 hours around the clock
discontinue the albuterol to prevent tolerance

questions.rationale: Using a SABA more than 2 days per week, nighttime awakenings, frequent refills, and PEF below 80% of personal best indicate asthma that is not well controlled. questions.stem: An 81-year-old client with COPD and arthritis in both hands is prescribed an albuterol metered-dose inhaler. During a return demonstration, the client sprays the dose, then inhales 2 seconds later, and a visible mist escapes from the mouth. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Teach the client to hold the inhaler 2 inches from the open mouth
Request a prescription for a spacer (valved holding chamber)
Tell the client to take 4 puffs instead of 2 to compensate
Suggest the client inhale the dose through the nose
optionRationales: Incorrect — the open-mouth technique still requires precise coordination, which this client lacks.
Correct — a spacer holds the medication so the client does not need to coordinate actuation and inhalation, improving lung deposition.
Incorrect — increasing the dose without a prescription is unsafe and does not fix the technique.
Incorrect — inhalers are designed for oral inhalation to reach the lower airways.
questions.rationale: Older adults often have difficulty coordinating MDI actuation with inhalation because of arthritis, weakness, or cognitive changes. A spacer or valved holding chamber allows the client to press the canister and then inhale slowly, increasing the dose reaching the lungs and reducing oropharyngeal deposition.
questions.takeaway: Poor hand–breath coordination with an MDI? Add a spacer.
questions.hintContent: Recall the purpose of a spacer and the coordination skill an MDI requires.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the specific technique error in the stem and choose the option that removes that problem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a left chest tube connected to a dry-suction chest drainage unit prescribed at –20 cm H₂O. The suction control dial is set at –20 cm H₂O and the unit is connected to wall suction, but the suction indicator (bellows/float) is not expanded. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Add sterile water to the suction control chamber up to the 20 cm line
Clamp the chest tube and replace the drainage unit
Raise the wall suction until the indicator appears
Turn the suction control dial up to –40 cm H₂O until bubbling starts
optionRationales: Incorrect — dry-suction units do not use water in the suction control chamber.
Incorrect — clamping risks tension pneumothorax, and the unit is not malfunctioning.
Correct — in a dry-suction unit, the dial sets the amount of suction; the wall source must be high enough (commonly at least –80 mm Hg) to activate the indicator.
Incorrect — the dial controls the prescribed amount of suction and should not be changed without an order.
questions.rationale: In dry-suction systems the regulator dial determines the suction level applied to the pleural space, and a visual indicator confirms suction is being delivered. If the indicator is not visible, the wall source is too low. The nurse increases the wall source (not the dial) until the indicator appears, and checks connections for leaks.
questions.takeaway: Dry suction: the dial sets the level; the wall source must be high enough to trigger the indicator.
questions.hintContent: Recall the difference between wet- and dry-suction control systems and what the indicator tells you.
questions.hintStrategy: Figure out which part of the system is not doing its job; avoid options that change a prescribed setting or add risk.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client had a chest tube inserted 2 days ago for a spontaneous pneumothorax. On the previous shift, the water seal chamber showed intermittent bubbling with exhalation. Now the nurse notes continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber. The client's respirations are 18/min and unlabored, and SpO₂ is 96%. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Check the dressing and all tubing connections for a leak
Clamp the chest tube near the insertion site and leave it clamped for 1 hour
Document the finding as expected during lung re-expansion
Increase the suction level to remove the air more quickly
optionRationales: Correct — a new continuous air leak often comes from a loose connection or dislodged tube; the nurse checks the dressing and all connections first.
Incorrect — prolonged clamping without an order can cause tension pneumothorax.
Incorrect — continuous bubbling is not expected; intermittent bubbling with exhalation or coughing is.
Incorrect — changing suction requires an order and does not locate the leak.
questions.rationale: Intermittent bubbling with exhalation or cough means air is still leaving the pleural space. A change to continuous bubbling suggests a system leak (loose connection, crack, tube pulled back with an eyelet outside the chest). Because the client is stable, the nurse inspects the insertion site and connections first; if the leak cannot be found, the provider is notified.
questions.takeaway: New continuous bubbling in the water seal = check for a leak, starting at the client and working toward the unit.
questions.hintContent: Recall what intermittent versus continuous bubbling in the water seal chamber indicates.
questions.hintStrategy: The client is stable, so gather data about the equipment before making changes. Eliminate options that are unsafe or require an order.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client has had a right chest tube to water seal for 4 days after a pneumothorax. The nurse notes that the water level in the water seal chamber no longer fluctuates with breathing. The tubing has no kinks or dependent loops, breath sounds are equal bilaterally, SpO₂ is 97% on room air, and today's chest x-ray shows full lung re-expansion. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: The tubing is occluded by a clot and should be stripped
The drainage unit has lost its water seal and must be replaced
A tension pneumothorax is developing on the right side
The lung has most likely re-expanded
optionRationales: Incorrect — there are no signs of obstruction, and stripping is not recommended.
Incorrect — tidaling requires the water seal; there is no evidence it has been lost.
Incorrect — equal breath sounds, normal SpO₂, and x-ray re-expansion rule this out.
Correct — when the lung fully re-expands, pleural pressure changes no longer transmit to the water seal, so tidaling stops.
questions.rationale: Tidaling reflects pressure changes in the pleural space during breathing. It stops either when the tubing is obstructed or when the lung has re-expanded. With patent tubing, a stable client, and x-ray confirmation, the cessation of tidaling indicates re-expansion; the nurse documents and reports it, anticipating a plan for tube removal.
questions.takeaway: No tidaling + patent tube + re-expanded lung on x-ray = the chest tube has done its job.
questions.hintContent: Recall the two main reasons tidaling in the water seal chamber stops.
questions.hintStrategy: Use every piece of data in the stem to rule out the dangerous causes before choosing an interpretation.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to assist the provider with removing a client's chest tube. Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Administer the prescribed analgesic about 30 minutes before removal
Instruct the client to breathe in and out deeply while the tube is pulled
Teach the client to take a deep breath and hold it (or bear down) as the tube is removed
Have an airtight petrolatum gauze dressing ready to cover the site immediately
Clamp the chest tube for 24 hours before removal as a routine step
Monitor for dyspnea and decreased SpO₂ after removal
optionRationales: Correct — chest tube removal is painful; premedication improves comfort and cooperation.
Incorrect — inhaling while the tube is withdrawn can draw air into the pleural space.
Correct — breath-holding or a Valsalva maneuver keeps intrathoracic pressure positive and prevents air entry.
Correct — an occlusive dressing seals the site to prevent air from entering.
Incorrect — clamping is done only if specifically prescribed (e.g., a clamp trial), not routinely.
Correct — recurrent pneumothorax can occur; a follow-up chest x-ray is usually ordered.
questions.rationale: Safe chest tube removal involves premedication, having the client hold the breath or perform a Valsalva maneuver during removal, immediately sealing the site with an occlusive dressing, and monitoring for recurrence of pneumothorax (dyspnea, decreased breath sounds, falling SpO₂) with a follow-up x-ray.
questions.takeaway: Chest tube out: premedicate, breath-hold, seal the site, and watch for recurrence.
questions.hintContent: Recall how intrathoracic pressure changes during inspiration and why that matters when an opening is created in the chest wall.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option ask: would this let air into the pleural space or prevent it? Judge each option independently.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients with chest tubes. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with a pneumothorax who has intermittent bubbling in the water seal chamber when coughing
A client 4 hours after lobectomy with 180 mL of bright red drainage in the past hour
A client with a chest tube for 3 days who requests pain medication for a pain level of 5/10
A client with a small area of crepitus around the insertion site that was marked with a pen yesterday and has not spread beyond the marked borders
optionRationales: Incorrect — intermittent bubbling with coughing is expected while air is evacuating.
Correct — a sudden increase to more than 100 mL/hr of bright red drainage suggests active bleeding and possible hemorrhage.
Incorrect — pain needs attention but is not life-threatening.
Incorrect — stable, marked subcutaneous emphysema that is not spreading is not a priority.
questions.rationale: Chest tube drainage greater than 100 mL/hr, especially bright red, indicates possible hemorrhage and threatens circulation; the provider must be notified promptly. The other findings are expected or stable.
questions.takeaway: Chest tube drainage > 100 mL/hr or suddenly bright red = possible hemorrhage; see that client first.
questions.hintContent: Recall the drainage volume threshold that must be reported and which chest tube findings are expected.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare 'expected/stable' against 'new and worsening'; choose the client with an acute change that threatens airway, breathing, or circulation.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: A client with a chest tube connected to suction for a pneumothorax is being prepared for a walk in the hallway, as prescribed. The provider's order allows the tube to be placed to water seal for ambulation. For each action, indicate whether it is appropriate or not appropriate.
rows: Clamp the chest tube during the walk to prevent backflow
Disconnect the unit from wall suction and leave the suction port open to air
Keep the drainage unit upright and below the level of the chest
Coil excess tubing on the bed and avoid dependent loops before and after the walk
Hold the drainage unit at shoulder height so the tubing does not drag
optionRationales: Not appropriate — clamping traps air in the pleural space and can cause tension pneumothorax.
Appropriate — the water seal still prevents air entry; leaving the suction port open allows air to vent.
Appropriate — gravity drainage requires the unit to stay upright and below chest level.
Appropriate — dependent loops fill with fluid and impede drainage.
Not appropriate — raising the unit above the chest allows drainage to flow back into the pleural space.
questions.rationale: A chest drainage system can safely be taken off suction and placed to water seal for ambulation when prescribed. The nurse never clamps the tube for routine transport, keeps the unit upright and below the chest, leaves the suction port open to vent air, and prevents dependent loops.
questions.takeaway: Walking with a chest tube: water seal yes, clamp no, unit below the chest.
questions.hintContent: Recall the role of the water seal and why gravity matters in chest drainage.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide for each action whether it keeps the one-way valve and gravity drainage working, or disrupts them.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with emphysema calls the nurse after a coughing spell, reporting sudden sharp left-sided chest pain that worsens with breathing. The nurse finds diminished breath sounds and decreased chest wall movement on the left, RR 30/min, and SpO₂ 86% on 2 L/min. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {0}, which likely occurred because {1}, causing loss of {2} pressure in the pleural space.

options: secondary spontaneous pneumothorax
acute pulmonary edema
right-sided heart failure
pleural effusion
a bulla on the lung surface ruptured
fluid shifted from the capillaries
a blood clot lodged in the pulmonary artery
the diaphragm became paralyzed
negative
positive
osmotic
hydrostatic

questions.rationale: Clients with emphysema have enlarged, weakened air spaces (bullae/blebs) that can rupture, especially with coughing, allowing air into the pleural space. This is a secondary spontaneous pneumothorax. The normally negative intrapleural pressure that holds the lung against the chest wall is lost, and the lung collapses, causing sudden pleuritic pain, decreased breath sounds, and asymmetric chest movement on the affected side.
questions.takeaway: COPD + sudden one-sided pleuritic pain and diminished breath sounds = think ruptured bulla → pneumothorax.
questions.hintContent: Recall the lung-tissue changes of emphysema and what normally keeps the lung inflated against the chest wall.
questions.hintStrategy: Notice the unilateral findings and sudden pleuritic pain; that pattern narrows the condition, and the mechanism blanks must fit it.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse is preparing discharge teaching for a 24-year-old client who was treated with a chest tube for a first primary spontaneous pneumothorax. The client smokes cigarettes and enjoys scuba diving. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Seek emergency care for sudden chest pain or shortness of breath
Stopping smoking reduces the risk of another pneumothorax
Avoid air travel until the provider confirms full resolution on x-ray
Scuba diving can be resumed as soon as the incision heals
Perform forceful Valsalva maneuvers daily to strengthen the lungs
Avoid all walking for 6 weeks to protect the lung
optionRationales: Correct — recurrence is common; sudden pain and dyspnea require immediate evaluation.
Correct — smoking significantly increases the risk of recurrence.
Correct — pressure changes during flight can enlarge residual air; clients are advised to wait until resolution is confirmed.
Incorrect — scuba diving is generally avoided permanently after pneumothorax unless definitive surgical treatment is done, due to barotrauma risk.
Incorrect — straining raises intrathoracic pressure and has no lung-strengthening benefit.
Incorrect — gradual activity such as walking is encouraged; strenuous activity and contact sports are limited as advised.
questions.rationale: After spontaneous pneumothorax, teaching focuses on recognizing recurrence, smoking cessation (a major modifiable risk factor), and avoiding activities with large pressure changes — air travel until cleared and scuba diving indefinitely unless definitive surgery is performed. Normal walking is encouraged.
questions.takeaway: After pneumothorax: stop smoking, no flying until cleared, no scuba diving, and return for sudden pain or dyspnea.
questions.hintContent: Recall how changes in ambient pressure affect trapped gas and which risk factor most strongly predicts recurrence.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each instruction independently: does it reduce the risk of recurrence or harm, or does it expose the client to pressure changes?

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse on a medical unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client with asthma whose peak flow is 76% of personal best after an albuterol treatment and who speaks in full sentences
A client with a chest tube for a pneumothorax that shows tidaling in the water seal chamber and 20 mL of serous drainage in 4 hours
A client with pneumonia who has become newly confused, with RR 30/min and BP 86/50 mm Hg
A client with COPD who is going home today and asks the nurse to review how to use the home oxygen concentrator
optionRationales: Incorrect — a yellow-zone peak flow that is improving after a SABA, with full sentences, shows a response to treatment; the client needs follow-up but is stable.
Incorrect — tidaling and a small amount of serous drainage are expected findings that show a patent, functioning system.

Correct — new confusion, tachypnea, and hypotension in a client with pneumonia suggest sepsis with impaired perfusion and tissue oxygenation; this client is unstable and needs immediate assessment and escalation.
Incorrect — discharge teaching is important but can wait until the unstable client has been assessed.
questions.rationale: Prioritize acute, unexpected changes over stable or routine needs. In a client with pneumonia, new confusion, a respiratory rate of 22/min or more, and a systolic BP of 100 mm Hg or less are warning signs of sepsis and tissue hypoxia (the qSOFA criteria). The asthma client is improving, the chest tube findings are expected, and discharge teaching can wait.
questions.takeaway: Pneumonia + new confusion + tachypnea + hypotension = possible sepsis; see this client first.
questions.hintContent: Recall the warning signs that pneumonia is progressing to sepsis and impaired tissue oxygenation, and which chest tube findings are expected.
questions.hintStrategy: For each client ask: is this finding expected or improving, or is it a new, unstable change? Choose acute and unstable over routine.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 79-year-old client who had a stroke 3 days ago and has mild dysphagia. The client is at risk for aspiration pneumonia. Which interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the head of the bed elevated at least 30° at all times unless contraindicated
Ensure a swallow screen is completed before giving oral food, fluids, or medications
Provide oral care at least twice daily
Encourage the client to drink thin liquids through a straw
Have the client sit upright with the chin tucked while swallowing
Place the client flat for 30 minutes after meals to aid digestion
optionRationales: Correct — head-of-bed elevation reduces reflux and aspiration.
Correct — a swallow screen identifies dysphagia before anything is given by mouth.
Correct — oral care reduces the bacterial load that can be aspirated into the lungs.
Incorrect — straws and thin liquids increase the speed and volume of fluid reaching the pharynx, raising aspiration risk in dysphagia.
Correct — upright positioning with a chin tuck helps protect the airway during swallowing.
Incorrect — the client should remain upright for at least 30 minutes after eating.
questions.rationale: Older adults and clients after a stroke have diminished cough and gag reflexes and increased risk of aspiration pneumonia. Evidence-based prevention includes swallow screening, upright positioning with a chin tuck, head-of-bed elevation, oral hygiene, and avoiding thin liquids through straws unless cleared by speech-language pathology.
questions.takeaway: Prevent aspiration: screen the swallow, sit up, tuck the chin, clean the mouth, skip the straw.
questions.hintContent: Recall how aging and stroke affect cough, gag, and swallow reflexes, and what reduces the volume of oral bacteria aspirated.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as true/false: does it protect the airway during and after eating, or does it increase the chance of material entering the trachea?

  • Blood cultures ×2 sets

questions.stem: A client is admitted with suspected community-acquired pneumonia. Refer to the Admission Orders and Vital Signs. Which order should the nurse implement first?
options: Administer acetaminophen 650 mg PO
Administer ceftriaxone 1 g IV
Obtain blood cultures
Administer azithromycin 500 mg IV
optionRationales: Incorrect — fever reduction improves comfort but does not take priority over time-sensitive culture collection before antibiotics.
Incorrect — antibiotics should be started promptly, but cultures must be drawn first so the antibiotic does not interfere with organism growth.
Correct — obtaining cultures before the first antibiotic dose allows accurate identification of the organism; antibiotics should follow without delay.
Incorrect — like ceftriaxone, it should be given after cultures are obtained.
questions.rationale: Blood and sputum cultures should be obtained before the first antibiotic dose because antibiotics can sterilize cultures and prevent identification of the pathogen and its sensitivities. Cultures must not delay antibiotic therapy — the nurse obtains them quickly and then administers antibiotics promptly.
questions.takeaway: Cultures before antibiotics — then give the antibiotics without delay.
questions.hintContent: Recall why the timing of specimen collection relative to antibiotics matters for culture results.
questions.hintStrategy: All orders are appropriate; determine which one becomes impossible to do correctly if done later.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client with COPD who already uses pursed-lip breathing reports becoming very short of breath while climbing stairs at home. The nurse teaches diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing. Complete the following sentence by choosing from the lists of options.
questions.template: The nurse instructs the client to place one hand on the {0} and inhale slowly through the nose so that {1}, then exhale slowly while {2}.

options: upper chest
abdomen
lower back
side of the neck
the shoulders lift toward the ears
the abdomen rises while the chest stays still
the neck muscles tighten with each breath
the chest and abdomen both stay still
gently tightening the abdominal muscles
holding the breath for 30 seconds first
forcing the air out as hard as possible
raising the shoulders to open the chest

questions.rationale: Diaphragmatic breathing shifts the work of breathing to the diaphragm and away from the neck and shoulder accessory muscles, which lowers the work of breathing. The client places one hand on the abdomen and one on the chest, inhales slowly through the nose so the abdomen rises while the chest stays relatively still, and exhales slowly (often through pursed lips) while gently tightening the abdominal muscles to move the diaphragm up. Forceful exhalation and prolonged breath-holding worsen air trapping and dyspnea.
questions.takeaway: Diaphragmatic breathing: hand on the belly, belly rises on the way in, gentle abdominal tightening on the way out.
questions.hintContent: Recall which muscle should do most of the work of quiet breathing and which muscles are overused during dyspnea in COPD.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the hand position first; the next blanks must describe what that hand should feel during inhalation and exhalation.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 19-year-old client with asthma has a personal best peak expiratory flow (PEF) of 400 L/min. The nurse reviews the client's home log using the asthma action plan. For each entry, indicate the zone it represents.
rows: Tuesday: PEF 280 L/min, coughing and mild chest tightness
Wednesday: PEF 180 L/min, trouble walking and talking
Thursday: PEF 330 L/min, slept through the night
Friday: PEF 300 L/min, woke at night coughing
optionRationales: Green — 360 is 90% of personal best with no symptoms.
Yellow — 280 is 70% of personal best with symptoms; use quick-relief medication and follow the plan.
Red — 180 is 45% of personal best with difficulty walking and talking; take rescue medication and seek emergency care.
Green — 330 is about 83% of personal best (≥ 80%) without night symptoms.
Yellow — 300 is 75% of personal best, and night waking indicates worsening control.
questions.rationale: Asthma action plan zones are based on percentage of personal best PEF and symptoms: green ≥ 80% (continue controller), yellow 50%–79% (caution: add quick-relief medication, contact provider if not improving), red < 50% (medical alert: rescue medication and emergency care).
questions.takeaway: PEF zones: green ≥ 80%, yellow 50%–79%, red < 50% of personal best.
questions.hintContent: Recall the percentage cutoffs for the green, yellow, and red zones of an asthma action plan.
questions.hintStrategy: Convert each PEF to a percentage of 400, then check whether the symptoms agree with that zone.
