questions.stem: A client at 10 weeks' gestation who has moderate persistent asthma well controlled with budesonide says, 'I stopped my steroid inhaler because I don't want to hurt the baby. I'll just use albuterol if I need it.' Which response by the nurse is best?
options: 'Stopping the inhaler is reasonable during the first trimester when the baby's organs are forming.'
'Poorly controlled asthma lowers your baby's oxygen; your inhaler is the safer choice.'
'You can switch to oral prednisone tablets, which are safer for the baby than any inhaled medication.'
'Albuterol alone will control your asthma as long as you use it every 4 hours.'
optionRationales: Incorrect — stopping controller therapy risks exacerbations and maternal/fetal hypoxemia.
Correct — maternal hypoxemia from poorly controlled asthma poses a greater risk to the fetus than inhaled corticosteroids; budesonide has the most safety data in pregnancy.
Incorrect — systemic steroids have more adverse effects than inhaled steroids and are used for exacerbations, not routine control.
Incorrect — SABA-only therapy does not treat airway inflammation and increases exacerbation risk.
questions.rationale: During pregnancy, the fetus depends on maternal oxygenation. Uncontrolled asthma increases the risk of preeclampsia, preterm birth, and low birth weight. Inhaled corticosteroids, especially budesonide, are considered safe and should be continued; management involves both the pulmonologist/primary provider and the obstetrician.
questions.takeaway: In pregnancy, well-controlled asthma protects the baby — keep the controller inhaler.
questions.hintContent: Recall how maternal oxygenation affects the fetus and which asthma medication has the most safety data in pregnancy.
questions.hintStrategy: Weigh the risk of the drug against the risk of the disease. Choose the response that corrects the misconception while supporting the client's goal of protecting the baby.

tabs.title: Home Health Visit
tabs.html:
Baseline (last month): SpO₂ 91% on 2 L/min; uses albuterol about twice weekly; white sputum in the morning; walks to mailbox without stopping.

Today: SpO₂ 87% on 2 L/min; used albuterol 5 times since yesterday; sputum thick and green, more than usual; had to stop twice walking to the bathroom. Barrel-shaped chest, clubbed fingers, and pursed-lip breathing noted. T 37.8 °C (100 °F).

questions.stem: The home health nurse visits a 68-year-old client with COPD. Refer to the Home Health Visit note. Which findings indicate that the client may be experiencing an acute exacerbation of COPD? Select all that apply.
options: SpO₂ 87% on 2 L/min
Increased use of albuterol
Thick green sputum in greater amounts
Barrel-shaped chest
Clubbed fingers
Pursed-lip breathing
Needing to stop while walking to the bathroom
optionRationales: Indicates exacerbation — SpO₂ is lower than the client's baseline of 91% on the same oxygen flow.
Indicates exacerbation — increased rescue medication use shows worsening symptoms.
Indicates exacerbation — increased sputum volume and purulence are cardinal signs of an exacerbation.
Chronic finding — barrel chest reflects long-standing hyperinflation.
Chronic finding — clubbing develops from chronic hypoxemia over months to years.
Chronic finding — pursed-lip breathing is a learned compensatory technique.
Indicates exacerbation — decreased activity tolerance compared with baseline shows increased dyspnea.
questions.rationale: A COPD exacerbation is an acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond day-to-day variation — increased dyspnea, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence — often with more rescue inhaler use and lower SpO₂ than baseline. Barrel chest, clubbing, and pursed-lip breathing are chronic findings that do not indicate an acute change.
questions.takeaway: COPD exacerbation = worse than THIS client's baseline: more dyspnea, more sputum, more purulent sputum.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three cardinal symptoms of a COPD exacerbation and which physical findings develop over years.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare 'Today' with 'Baseline.' Select only findings that CHANGED; chronic findings are present in both.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 22-year-old client arrives in the emergency department with an acute asthma exacerbation: speaking in phrases, RR 30/min, diffuse wheezes, SpO₂ 89% on room air. The provider prescribes oxygen, albuterol by nebulizer, and prednisone 50 mg PO. Place the actions in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Position the client upright
Apply oxygen and titrate to an SpO₂ of 93%–95%
Administer the albuterol nebulizer treatment
Administer prednisone 50 mg PO
Reassess breath sounds, work of breathing, SpO₂, and peak flow
questions.rationale: Upright positioning is immediate and improves ventilation. Oxygen corrects hypoxemia (GINA target SpO₂ 93%–95% in adults). A short-acting beta₂-agonist relieves bronchospasm within minutes. Systemic corticosteroids should be given early (within the first hour), but act over hours to reduce inflammation. The nurse then reassesses the response to treatment.
questions.takeaway: Acute asthma: sit up → oxygen → SABA → steroid → reassess.
questions.hintContent: Recall how quickly each intervention works and which directly addresses hypoxemia versus bronchospasm versus inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Order by speed and immediacy of benefit to airway and breathing; evaluation comes last.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: During an annual visit, a 46-year-old client who smokes 1 pack per day says, 'My dad just had a heart attack. I want to quit within the next month, but I've failed before.' Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Help the client set a quit date and choose cessation aids
Explain the long-term health consequences of continued smoking in detail, including heart disease
Encourage the client to cut down gradually over the next year
Document the client's smoking status and revisit it at the next annual visit
optionRationales: Correct — the client is ready to quit; the 'Assist' step of the 5 A's includes setting a quit date, a plan, behavioral support, and pharmacotherapy.
Incorrect — the client is already motivated; motivational information (the 5 R's) is for clients not ready to quit.
Incorrect — a year-long reduction without a quit plan is less effective than planned cessation with support.
Incorrect — delaying assistance misses a teachable moment.
questions.rationale: The 5 A's (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange) guide cessation counseling. This client is ready to quit, so the nurse assists by helping develop a plan with a quit date, providing referral to counseling or a quitline, and discussing medications such as NRT, varenicline, or bupropion. Combining counseling with medication gives the best success rate.
questions.takeaway: Ready to quit? Assist: set a date, make a plan, add counseling and medication.
questions.hintContent: Recall the 5 A's of tobacco cessation and what distinguishes a client who is ready to quit from one who is not.
questions.hintStrategy: Determine the client's stage of readiness from the stem first, then choose the action that matches that stage.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client is prescribed varenicline for smoking cessation, with a quit date set for 1 week after starting the medication. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: 'I will keep smoking this week and stop on my quit date.'
'I'll report it if I feel depressed or notice unusual changes in my mood.'
'I'll take my pills on an empty stomach so they absorb better.'
'I might have strange dreams, so I'll take my evening dose after dinner rather than at bedtime.'
optionRationales: Incorrect — varenicline is typically started 1 week before the quit date, so continued smoking during that week is expected.
Incorrect — reporting neuropsychiatric changes is correct teaching.
Correct — varenicline should be taken after eating with a full glass of water to reduce nausea, its most common adverse effect.
Incorrect — taking the evening dose earlier can reduce insomnia and vivid dreams; this shows understanding.
questions.rationale: Varenicline, a partial nicotinic receptor agonist, is started 1 week before the quit date. It should be taken after meals with a full glass of water to minimize nausea. Clients should be taught about insomnia and vivid dreams and to report mood or behavior changes.
questions.takeaway: Varenicline: start a week before quitting, take after food with water, report mood changes.
questions.hintContent: Recall the most common adverse effect of varenicline and how administration can reduce it.
questions.hintStrategy: This is a 'needs further teaching' item — look for the INCORRECT statement.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A 55-year-old client with COPD who smokes asks which vaccines are recommended to prevent respiratory infections and complications. The client has never received a pneumococcal vaccine and had a tetanus booster 12 years ago. Which vaccines should the nurse recommend? Select all that apply.
options: Inactivated influenza vaccine injection every year
Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine
Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria, acellular pertussis) vaccine
Live attenuated intranasal influenza vaccine
BCG vaccine to prevent tuberculosis
optionRationales: Correct — annual influenza vaccination is recommended for everyone 6 months and older, especially clients with chronic lung disease.
Correct — pneumococcal conjugate vaccination is recommended for adults 50 and older and for younger adults with chronic lung disease or who smoke.
Correct — a Tdap or Td booster is due every 10 years; pertussis protection is valuable for clients with lung disease.
Incorrect — the live nasal influenza vaccine is approved only through age 49 and is not preferred for clients with chronic lung disease.
Incorrect — BCG is not routinely used in the United States.
questions.rationale: Vaccination is a key health-promotion intervention for clients with chronic lung disease. Recommended vaccines include annual inactivated influenza vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV20 or PCV21 alone, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23), and a Tdap/Td booster every 10 years. Live nasal influenza vaccine is not indicated at this age, and BCG is not part of routine U.S. adult immunization.
questions.takeaway: COPD health promotion: flu shot yearly, pneumococcal vaccine, and pertussis protection.
questions.hintContent: Recall CDC adult immunization recommendations for adults with chronic lung disease, including age limits on live vaccines.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each option against the client's age and diagnosis; a vaccine can be wrong because of age limits even if it targets a respiratory illness.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a 4-year-old client with asthma who has had three ED visits this year. The parent says, 'I only smoke in the car with the windows down or outside, never around my child.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: 'That's a good plan. Smoking outside the home and away from your child completely protects your child's lungs.'
'Opening the car windows is enough to clear the smoke before your child rides.'
'Your child should use the rescue inhaler before riding in the car.'
'Smoke residue in the car and on clothes can still trigger asthma. Can we talk about quitting?'
optionRationales: Incorrect — smoke residue on clothing, hair, and surfaces (thirdhand smoke) still exposes the child.
Incorrect — car interiors retain smoke particles and residue even with windows open.
Incorrect — premedicating does not remove the trigger and normalizes ongoing exposure.
Correct — this corrects the misconception about exposure and opens a nonjudgmental conversation about cessation, the most effective protection.
questions.rationale: Children are more vulnerable to tobacco smoke because of smaller airways and higher respiratory rates. Secondhand and thirdhand smoke (residue on surfaces, clothing, and car interiors) are asthma triggers. The best protection is a smoke-free home and car and parental cessation; the nurse should address this respectfully and offer support.
questions.takeaway: No 'safe' place to smoke around an asthmatic child — residue travels on clothes and in cars.
questions.hintContent: Recall how tobacco smoke exposure affects children's airways and the concept of thirdhand smoke.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the response that both corrects the misconception and keeps communication therapeutic and nonjudgmental.

'Using my wood-burning fireplace every evening will keep the air warm and dry for my lungs.'
'I'll use a HEPA air filter in my bedroom.'
'I'll spray aerosol air fresheners to cover odors that bother my breathing.'
'I'll ask my family not to smoke inside the house or car.'
optionRationales: Shows understanding — limiting outdoor activity on poor air-quality days reduces exposure to pollutants.
Needs further teaching — wood smoke contains particulate matter that irritates airways and triggers exacerbations.
Shows understanding — HEPA filtration reduces indoor particulates and allergens.
Needs further teaching — aerosol sprays and strong scents are airway irritants.
Shows understanding — eliminating secondhand smoke in the home and car reduces irritant exposure.
questions.rationale: Airborne irritants such as cigarette smoke, wood smoke, pollution, and chemical sprays trigger airway inflammation. Managing environmental air quality — monitoring the air quality index, filtering indoor air, and avoiding smoke and aerosols — reduces exposure and exacerbations.
questions.takeaway: Protect the airway at home: no smoke, no aerosols, filter the air, watch the air quality index.
questions.hintContent: Recall the airborne irritants listed in Module 15's health promotion content and how they affect the airways.

questions.rationale: Pack-years = packs per day × years smoked (1.5 × 20 = 30). The USPSTF (2021) recommends annual low-dose CT screening for adults aged 50–80 who have at least a 20-pack-year history and currently smoke or quit within the past 15 years. Screening is for asymptomatic clients, and quitting 8 years ago does not remove eligibility.
questions.takeaway: Lung cancer screening: age 50–80, ≥ 20 pack-years, current smoker or quit ≤ 15 years ago.

questions.stem: A client who stopped smoking 4 days ago calls the clinic reporting irritability, trouble concentrating, increased appetite, and a cough that seems 'worse than when I smoked.' The client asks whether to start smoking again. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: 'These are expected withdrawal effects, and coughing often increases as your airways clear.'
'Your symptoms mean you quit too quickly; cutting back gradually over several months would work better.'
'These are signs of a respiratory infection, so you should come in today to be started on antibiotics.'
'A worsening cough after quitting usually means permanent lung damage has already occurred.'
optionRationales: Correct — nicotine withdrawal peaks in the first several days and fades over weeks; as cilia recover, the cough can temporarily increase to clear mucus.
Incorrect — abrupt quitting is effective; symptoms are expected and do not mean the approach failed.
Incorrect — without fever or purulent sputum, these findings fit withdrawal and recovery, not infection.
Incorrect — this is inaccurate and may discourage the client from continuing.
questions.rationale: Nicotine withdrawal symptoms (irritability, anxiety, difficulty concentrating, increased appetite, insomnia) peak within the first few days and subside over 2–4 weeks. Smoking paralyzes and damages cilia; as ciliary function returns, a temporary increase in cough helps clear accumulated mucus. The nurse reassures, reinforces the benefits, and suggests coping strategies or NRT.
questions.takeaway: A 'quitter's cough' is a sign of healing cilia, not failure.
questions.hintContent: Recall how smoking affects cilia and the typical timeline of nicotine withdrawal.
questions.hintStrategy: Interpret the symptoms in the context of the recent change (quitting), and choose the response that is accurate and supports continued abstinence.
